proposal: The Mandate recommends breaking up and downsizing NOAA, arguing that many of its functions could be provided commercially. Specific steps include focusing the National Weather Service on data gathering and fully commercializing its forecasting, disbanding most climate research in the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) and consolidating its labs, moving National Ocean Service survey work to the Coast Guard and USGS, streamlining the overlapping goals of NOAA Fisheries and the Fish and Wildlife Service, and breaking up the Office of Marine and Aviation Operations with its assets reassigned to GSA or other agencies.
remaining: Congress would need to enact the elimination or transfer of OAR and other statutory NOAA offices; the FY2027 appropriations outcome is pending.
Commercialization of National Weather Service forecasting: no formal step found.

Transfer of ocean survey work to the Coast Guard and USGS and breakup of the marine and aviation office: no action found (NOAA's FY2027 justification funds uncrewed systems and fleet recapitalization while trimming flight hours, aircraft recapitalization and the NOAA Corps, and the portions read do not mention the Coast Guard).
Adoption of the proposed move of protected-species duties to Fish and Wildlife.

status_summary: Staffing reductions in 2025 are operative: CRS reports NOAA's funded workforce fell from over 12,200 full-time equivalents in FY2024 to just over 11,000 in FY2026, and NPR reported the National Weather Service lost roughly 500 to 600 positions before it began rehiring in June 2025. The structural changes have not been enacted. The FY2026 request (June 2025) and the FY2027 request (April 2026) both propose eliminating OAR and moving some of its work to the weather and ocean services, and the FY2026 request also proposes moving Endangered Species Act and marine mammal duties to Fish and Wildlife. Congress kept OAR in the FY2026 appropriations law (P.L. 119-74, signed 2026-01-23, NOAA at about $6.17 billion), and the House committee's FY2027 bill again retains OAR. NOAA's FY2027 budget justification (April 2026) proposes about 1,520 terminated positions and a decrease of roughly 19 percent in discretionary appropriations, advances the Fish and Wildlife Service transfer, and shows National Weather Service positions rising slightly; the portions read describe more use of commercial data, not commercialization of forecasting, and no formal step to commercialize National Weather Service forecasting was found.

timeline.event: NOAA's FY2026 congressional budget submission (posted under a June 2025 path; exact day not confirmed) proposes eliminating OAR as a line office, moving some activities to the National Ocean Service and National Weather Service, ending many OAR programs, and moving Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act functions to the Fish and Wildlife Service. It describes using commercial industry capabilities for weather but does not propose commercializing forecasts.

NPR reports that the National Weather Service lost roughly 500 to 600 positions to 2025 cuts (including about 100 probationary terminations) and, under a hiring-freeze exemption, begins hiring more than 100 staff (126 positions per the union) to stabilize field offices.

AP reports that NWS and NOAA downsizing coincides with appointees who have ties to private weather firms, and notes the Mandate's call to fully commercialize forecasting. The reporting describes no formal commercialization decision.
Senate confirms Neil Jacobs as NOAA Administrator (date reflects the report's publication; the vote date was not separately confirmed).

P.L. 119-74 (FY2026 Commerce, Justice, Science and related appropriations) is signed. NOAA receives about $6.17 billion; Congress keeps OAR and moves some OAR programs to the National Weather Service.

NOAA's FY2027 congressional budget justification (posted under an April 2026 path; the first of the month is used because the day is not confirmed) requests $4.54 billion in discretionary appropriations, about 19 percent below the FY2026 enacted $5.63 billion, and cuts NOAA positions from 11,929 to 10,208 (FTE from 11,210 to 9,693). It shows OAR at zero positions and dollars, terminating its climate, weather and ocean laboratories and cooperative institutes and Sea Grant and moving ocean exploration, observations and acidification work to the National Ocean Service and supercomputing to the National Weather Service; it advances the transfer of Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act functions to the Fish and Wildlife Service, moves the Office of Space Commerce to Departmental Management, raises National Weather Service positions from 4,473 to 4,499, and describes more use of commercially available data rather than commercializing NWS forecasting. For the aviation and marine office it funds uncrewed systems and fleet recapitalization while trimming flight hours, aircraft recapitalization and the NOAA Corps.

At a House hearing on the FY2027 request, Administrator Jacobs defends the plan to end OAR, saying its in-house research would move to other NOAA offices while extramural research is cut. The news report gives a roughly 26 percent NOAA cut and says the request ends funding for the greenhouse gas monitoring network (NOAA's budget document shows a decrease of about 19 percent in discretionary appropriations; the two bases were not reconciled).

The House Appropriations Committee reports H.R. 8845, the FY2027 Commerce, Justice, Science appropriations bill (H.Rept. 119-652), with $4.01 billion from the general fund for NOAA Operations, Research, and Facilities, and a provision (Sec. 113) requiring the National Weather Service to maintain staffing levels to fulfill its mission to the maximum extent possible; the OAR treatment is described by CRS (see the 2026-07-28 entry), as the portion of the bill text read did not address OAR.

CRS summarizes the FY2027 request: eliminate OAR, cut about 1,500 more full-time equivalents, and cut the National Ocean Service and NMFS deeply. The House committee bill (H.Rept. 119-652) retains OAR at 2 percent below FY2026 and directs NOAA not to close its laboratories; no Senate bill had been introduced.

The NWS commercialization finding remains an absence finding in the portions read.
